findings.summary: The deck stops after the scaling chapter, covering 7 of the syllabus's 10 chapters, yet the caption advertises content and a page count that do not exist.
findings.evidence: Caption: "fan-out cost math, and the exact arithmetic that tells you to just poll instead. Ten pages, every gotcha we have paid for." — but the deck has 8 slides and its last section is "Scaling: Fan-Out, State, and Cost"; nothing on client-side caching/reconnects, the polling-vs-subscription arithmetic (`time_between_events > poll_interval`), or the gotchas/decision summary appears anywhere.
findings.fix: Either add the three missing chapters (Client-Side, When Polling Beats a Subscription, Gotchas/Testing/Summary) as pages 9-10, or rewrite the caption to describe only what ships: drop "Ten pages" and the polling-arithmetic and gotchas promises.

findings.summary: The deck names the most common silent failure — a payload not keyed by the field name — but never shows what a correctly keyed payload looks like, so the rule cannot be applied.
findings.evidence: "With no `resolve`, payload must be keyed by field name" / "Wrong key yields `null` with no error at all", while the adjacent code block only demonstrates the `resolve: (payload) => payload.message` path and never shows a no-`resolve` payload.
findings.fix: Add two contrasting lines to the code block, e.g. `// no resolve: publish({ messageAdded: message })` versus `// wrong: publish({ message }) -> data.messageAdded === null`.

findings.summary: The claim that subscription CPU cost is independent of write rate is false and contradicts the bullet directly above it.
findings.evidence: "One publish times N subscribers = N executions" ... "CPU grows with subscriber count, not with write rate"
findings.fix: Replace with "CPU grows with publish rate TIMES subscriber count — a doubling of either doubles executions" (matching the 'cost = query cost × event rate' point made two slides earlier).

findings.summary: Federated subscriptions are described as confined to a single subgraph, but only the root field is — the router does resolve the rest of the selection set across other subgraphs on every event.
findings.evidence: "Federated subscriptions resolve in one subgraph, router proxies" / "You cannot fan one subscription across subgraphs"
findings.fix: Change to: "The subscription ROOT field must live in one subgraph; the router opens the stream there and then fetches entity fields from other subgraphs per event. What you cannot do is split one root field's stream across subgraphs."

findings.summary: The root field is said to yield the raw event payload, which contradicts the accurate description of the subscribe/resolve pair on page 4.
findings.evidence: "Root field yields the raw event payload value" vs page 4's "`resolve` maps each raw event to the field value" / "With no `resolve`, payload must be keyed by field name"
findings.fix: Change to "The raw event payload becomes the root field's parent value; `resolve` (or the default `payload[fieldName]`) turns it into the field value."

findings.summary: WebSocket compression is characterised as per-frame with no cross-message history, but permessage-deflate retains the LZ77 window across messages unless no_context_takeover is negotiated.
findings.evidence: "gzip over a whole SSE stream beats per-frame deflate" / "Repetitive JSON compresses far better across frames"
findings.fix: Rewrite as: "permessage-deflate keeps its sliding window across messages by default (context takeover), so it also compresses repetitive JSON well — but servers that negotiate `server_no_context_takeover` to cap memory lose that, and a gzipped SSE stream then wins."

findings.summary: The "silent null" gotcha is stated unconditionally, but with the non-null root field the handbook itself declares, a mis-keyed payload produces an explicit execution error.
findings.evidence: "With no `resolve`, payload must be keyed by field name" / "Wrong key yields `null` with no error at all" — against page 1's `messageAdded(roomId: ID!): Message!`
findings.fix: Qualify it: "Wrong key yields `null` — silent if the field is nullable, and 'Cannot return null for non-nullable field' if it is declared `Message!`."

findings.summary: In the "Topic granularity" box, the long code token `MESSAGE_ADDED:roomId` cannot wrap, so it is pushed onto its own line — leaving an orphaned bullet marker above it — and runs the full inner width until it touches the box's right border.
findings.evidence: Box "Topic granularity" (right of the "vs" divider under "4. Filter Or Topic") renders as a line containing only "·", followed by "MESSAGE_ADDED:roomId" spanning from the box's left text inset to its right border with no visible right padding, unlike the sibling bullets "broker does routing" / "no wasted delivery" / "wrong topic = silence".
findings.fix: Give inline code inside these boxes a break opportunity (e.g. allow breaking on `_` and `:`, or `overflow-wrap: anywhere`) and keep the bullet marker on the same line as its first text run, so the token wraps inside the box instead of forcing a full-width line against the border.

findings.summary: `pubsub` is used in two code examples before pub/sub itself is introduced or the object's origin is explained.
findings.evidence: Page 4 code: `pubsub.asyncIterableIterator(`MSG_ADDED:${roomId}`)` and `await pubsub.publish(`MSG_ADDED:${id}`, {...})`; the first definition appears only on page 5: "`PubSub` from graphql-subscriptions is one EventEmitter".
findings.fix: Add one line before the resolver code on page 4 defining the object — e.g. "`pubsub` is the broker adapter: `publish(topic, payload)` in, an AsyncIterable out; backends compared on the next page."

findings.summary: The resolver example uses a per-room topic name as its answer before the section that poses the filter-versus-topic trade-off.
findings.evidence: Code block: "pubsub.asyncIterableIterator(`MSG_ADDED:${roomId}`),  // per-room topic" appears two blocks ahead of the "Filter Or Topic" cards that explain "Topic granularity … `MESSAGE_ADDED:roomId` … broker does routing".
findings.fix: Use the plain topic `MSG_ADDED` in the first resolver example and introduce the `:${roomId}` suffix in the "Filter Or Topic" section as the payoff of that comparison.

findings.summary: "Fan-out" is used as load-bearing terminology on three pages before it is defined.
findings.evidence: Page 4 card: "fan-out then discard"; page 5: "fire and forget fan-out"; the definition arrives only on page 7: "One publish times N subscribers = N executions".
findings.fix: Add a one-line gloss at first use on page 4 — e.g. "fan-out = one publish delivered to every matching subscriber" — or move the "Fan-Out Is The Number" definition bullet forward.

findings.summary: The payload-strategy table requires per-event authorization before authorization has been introduced anywhere in the deck.
findings.evidence: Page 5 table row: ["either way","per-event authz","re-check at delivery"]; authorization is first defined on page 6 — "Authorization must be re-checked continuously after that" / "For fat payloads, re-check rights at delivery time".
findings.fix: Drop the "per-event authz" row from the page 5 table (keeping thin/fat wire-and-price rows) and let the page 6 authorization section introduce delivery-time re-checking with the fat-payload leak risk it already states.

findings.summary: The recommended token-refresh mechanism — a custom client message — is not permitted by graphql-transport-ws, which closes the socket on any unrecognised message type.
findings.evidence: "Allow a client message carrying a refreshed token" / "That message updates the connection context in place" (protocol: "Receiving a message of a type or format which is not specified in this document will result in an immediate socket closure with the event 4400")
findings.fix: Say the refresh must ride an existing message type — the `Ping`/`Pong` payload field, which the protocol leaves free-form — or force a reconnect with a new `ConnectionInit`; a bespoke message type gets closed with 4400.
